body: A visiting worship leader in a hall in south London has taught the room a chorus he picked up from a recording. He has the words written out phonetically on a sheet, and he has set them, very carefully, to a tune of his own — four square bars, a rise at the end, the shape every chorus in his repertoire has. The room sings it twice. Two women near the front exchange a look somewhere in the middle of the second time through and then keep singing, because he means well and the tea is already made. Afterwards one of them tries to explain to him what he has just had a hall full of people say, and gets as far as the second syllable before both of them start laughing.

He had not sung it badly. He had sung a different sentence. Nothing in his training gave him any way of knowing that, because the thing he did wrong is not a thing that English is capable of doing wrong.
Yorùbá is a tonal language. Pitch is not expression laid over the top of the words; it is part of the words themselves, and the same syllable at a different pitch is a different item of vocabulary.

This is completely ordinary to any speaker, and it has an extraordinary consequence for music. A composer setting a Yorùbá text is not free to put any note under any syllable. The melody has to agree with the speech tones, or the line stops meaning what it said and starts meaning something else — usually something ridiculous, occasionally something worse. Put like that it sounds like a cage. In practice it works as an engine: the words arrive already carrying most of a melodic contour, so the tune is half written before anybody has sat down to write it, and what comes out is fused to the language at a level for which English has no equivalent at all.

There is a frequency for this on the band, and it is worth naming even though you cannot hear it tonight. HM 330.90 West Africa Inspire (Yorùbá) is assigned and in build — the number is held, the catalogue is being assembled, and nothing plays there yet.

That silence is also the reason the station has to be hosted rather than dubbed, which is the more expensive of the two routes by a considerable margin. A dubbed station needs a translator and an hour in a booth. A hosted one needs somebody who lives inside the language, who can hear a wrong note as a wrong word, and who is permitted to reject a track that is technically immaculate and tonally nonsense. There is no software for that judgement and there is no shortcut to acquiring it. Change the pitch and you have not changed the tune. You have changed the word.

The hymnbook habit runs deeper than anybody much likes to admit. For a long stretch of history the standard method of bringing a hymn into an African language was to keep the European tune and fit the new words to it, on the assumption that the tune was the vessel and the words were the cargo. Generations sang those hymns and loved them, and it would be graceless to sneer at that from here. But in a tonal language the method quietly guarantees a certain quantity of nonsense, and everybody involved learned to hear the nonsense as the ordinary price of singing in church. What that teaches, over a century, is that your own language is the part that bends.

It is also why the drums are not doing what a listener trained on Western music assumes they are doing. A talking drum can follow the tonal contour of speech closely enough to carry actual phrases, which means the instrument is not accompanying the praise so much as taking part in it, saying the same thing in a second register. Once you know that, a passage you had filed as a groove turns out to have been a sentence, and you can hear the singers answering it.
None of which survives a translation. The temptation at this point is to say that translation gets you most of the way there anyway. It does not.

Be fair to it first, because translation is honourable work and the faith is unthinkable without it. The Scriptures come to nearly everybody alive in a language other than the one they were written in, and something real crosses over every time. A translated lyric can carry doctrine accurately, and doctrine matters a great deal more than atmosphere. But a translated Yorùbá praise line is a strange object to be left holding. You keep the theology and you lose the mechanism, because the mechanism was never in the words on their own — it was in the fit between the words and the pitches, which is precisely the part that cannot travel. What is left is accurate and inert. It is a photograph of a joke.
Translation keeps what was said. In this language, the singing was part of what was said.

A man driving his daughter to a swimming lesson has a song on that his mother used to sing in her kitchen. His daughter is nine, her Yorùbá is thin and her English is not, and she asks him what one of the lines means. He starts to answer and stops. He tries again with different English words and stops again, and then there is a roundabout to deal with. In the end he does the only thing left available to him, which is to sing the line back to her, and then sing it once more, and she watches the side of his face instead of the road. Neither of them says anything else about it. She hums it wrong for a week, and then one Saturday, over the cereal, correctly.
He had not failed to translate it. There was nothing there to translate into; the line and its melody were one object, and the only way to hand it over was to hand the whole of it over at once.

Here is the honest cost, and it lands on you if you do not speak the language. A hosted station in a tongue you have no access to will give you very little of what a speaker gets from it. You will hear the shape and miss the sentence. You cannot join in, you cannot follow the argument a lyric is making, and there will be long stretches where you have no idea whether you are being taught, warned or congratulated. That is not a fault you can fix by concentrating harder.

But being outside a room is not at all the same as being shut out of it, and it does something to a listener that no amount of accessible material can. You are, for once, not the person the thing was made for, and you can hear perfectly well that it was made properly anyway. Almost everything any of us listens to has been arranged, at some level and by somebody, to suit us. An hour of praise built for other people, to standards you are in no position to audit, is a small and useful corrective to a very large assumption.

So the case for hosting rather than dubbing is not sentimental and it is not about representation. It is about what survives the journey. A Yorùbá praise line carries its meaning in the fit between pitch and syllable, and a station that renders it into English keeps the doctrine, loses the engine, and hands the listener something correct and dead. Hosting is slower to build, harder to staff and impossible to fake. It is also the only version that arrives with the music still inside it.
All of which you can test tonight, in a way, because the same phenomenon is already on air in another language.

The multilanguage block is the biggest thing on this dial — 40 stations across 29 languages, each hosted in its own tongue rather than translated into it afterwards. Several of those languages are tonal, which means the argument in this article is not a Yorùbá curiosity but a plain description of how a great deal of the world sings. If you have only ever heard worship in European languages, you have been listening to music in which the tune is free to go wherever the composer fancies, and you have almost certainly assumed that is simply what a tune is.

So start at HM 337.20 — Thailand Inspire (ไทย), which is on air now. Thai is a tonal language too, and although it is a long way from Yorùbá in every other respect, the same rule governs it: the melody has to agree with the words, or the words change underneath the singer. Put it on and listen to how the vocal line moves — the small steps, the contours that seem to be following something rather than deciding for themselves, the phrases that resolve where you would not have resolved them. You are hearing a melody that was not free. That constraint is the thing this article has been describing from the start, and it is audible tonight on a frequency that is actually playing, which is more than can be said for the one the article is about.

There is nothing to install and no card to find. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it starts — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it works on the hardware people actually own rather than the hardware a demo assumes. Add the page to your home screen if you want it a thumb away, and it opens like anything else on there. And do make an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band works out which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for — which is how the ones still in build get their turn.

Then, when you have had twenty minutes of a melody obeying a language, go back to whatever you normally listen to and notice how loose it is by comparison. That is not a criticism of it. It is just the difference showing. And when the Yorùbá frequency does open, you will arrive already knowing what the drums are for and why nobody is going to translate the chorus for you — which is a better preparation than any amount of being told.
